p.src: Now Li Yue led his troops forward, falsely claiming that Li Jue and Guo Si were pursuing the imperial carriage, greatly alarming the Emperor. Yang Feng said, “That is Li Yue.” He therefore ordered Xu Huang to ride out against him, and Li Yue personally came forth to fight. The two horsemen met, but in a single bout Xu Huang struck Li Yue from his saddle with one blow of his axe. He scattered and slew the remaining rebels, then escorted the imperial carriage safely through Ji Pass. Governor Zhang Yang prepared grain and silk and welcomed the imperial carriage at Zhi Road. The Emperor appointed Zhang Yang Grand Marshal. Zhang Yang then took leave of the Emperor and departed to station his troops at Yewang.

p.src: When the Emperor entered Luoyang, he found the palaces burned to the ground and the streets and markets desolate, with mugwort everywhere the eye could see. Nothing remained within the palace grounds but crumbling walls and ruined ramparts, so he ordered Yang Feng to erect a small temporary palace for his residence. When the civil and military officials offered their congratulations at court, they all stood amid thorns and brambles. An edict changed the Xingping era to the first year of Jian’an.

p.src: That year there was yet another great famine. Only a few hundred households remained in Luoyang, and with nothing to eat, all went outside the city to strip bark from trees and dig up grass roots for food. Even officials from the Gentleman of the Secretariat downward had to leave the city themselves to gather firewood and forage, and many died among the crumbling walls and ruined ramparts. p.src: Now Cao Cao, in Shandong, heard that the imperial carriage had returned to Luoyang and assembled his advisers for counsel. Xun Yu stepped forward and said, “In former times, Duke Wen of Jin restored King Xiang of Zhou, and the feudal lords submitted to him; Emperor Gaozu of Han mourned Emperor Yi, and the hearts of all under Heaven turned to him; today the Son of Heaven endures exile and hardship. If you, General, seize this moment to be the first to raise a righteous army and uphold the Emperor in accordance with the hopes of the people, it will be a strategy unequalled in any age. If you do not act quickly, someone else will forestall you.” Cao Cao was delighted. Just as he was preparing to muster his troops, a report suddenly came that an imperial envoy had arrived bearing an edict of summons. Cao Cao received the edict and fixed a day for the army to march.

p.src: Meanwhile, the Emperor remained in Luoyang, where nothing was ready and the city walls had collapsed; though he wished to repair them, he lacked the means. Then came a report that Li Jue and Guo Si were approaching at the head of their troops. The Emperor was greatly alarmed and asked Yang Feng, “The envoy to Shandong has not returned, yet the armies of Li Jue and Guo Si are upon us again. What are We to do?” Yang Feng and Han Xian said, “We are willing to fight the rebels to the death and protect Your Majesty.” Dong Cheng said, “The city walls are not strong and our troops and weapons are few. If we fight and fail to win, what then? It would be better to escort the imperial carriage eastward for the time being and take refuge in Shandong.” The Emperor followed his advice, and that very day the imperial carriage departed eastward for Shandong. The officials had no horses and all followed the imperial carriage on foot.

p.src: They had scarcely gone a bowshot beyond Luoyang when they saw clouds of dust blotting out the sun and heard gongs and drums shaking the sky as a vast host of men and horses approached. The Emperor and Empress trembled and could not speak. Suddenly a lone horseman came galloping toward them: it was the envoy previously sent to Shandong. Reaching the imperial carriage, he bowed and reported, “General Cao has mustered all the troops of Shandong and is coming in answer to the edict. Hearing that Li Jue and Guo Si were attacking Luoyang, he first sent Xiahou Dun as vanguard with ten senior generals and fifty thousand picked troops to protect Your Majesty.” Only then was the Emperor’s mind set at ease. Before long, Xiahou Dun arrived with Xu Chu, Dian Wei, and the others. They came before the imperial carriage to have audience with the Emperor and all saluted according to military ceremony. The Emperor had scarcely finished comforting and exhorting them when another report came that a second army was approaching from due east. The Emperor immediately ordered Xiahou Dun to investigate. He returned and reported, “It is Cao Cao’s infantry.”

May Your Majesty take good care of your sacred person and hold the welfare of the realm above all else.” The Emperor thereupon appointed Cao Cao Colonel Director of Retainers, granted him the imperial tally and battle-axe, and placed him in charge of the affairs of the Imperial Secretariat.

p.src: Now Li Jue and Guo Si, knowing that Cao Cao had come from afar, discussed giving battle at once. Jia Xu remonstrated, “You must not. Cao Cao’s soldiers are well trained and his generals valiant. It would be better to surrender to him and plead to be absolved of your crimes.” Li Jue angrily cried, “How dare you dampen our fighting spirit!” He drew his sword to behead Jia Xu, but the other generals persuaded him to spare the man. That night, Jia Xu rode off alone and returned to his native village.

p.src: The next day, Li Jue’s army advanced to meet Cao Cao’s forces. Cao Cao first ordered Xu Chu, Cao Ren, and Dian Wei to lead three hundred armored horsemen in three charges through Li Jue’s formation; only then did he draw up his battle lines. When the formations were complete, Li Jue’s nephews Li Xian and Li Bie rode out before the lines. Before either could speak, Xu Chu galloped forward and struck down Li Xian with a single stroke of his blade. Li Bie was so startled that he toppled backward from his horse. Xu Chu killed him as well and returned to his lines carrying a head in each hand. Cao Cao patted Xu Chu on the back and said, “You truly are my Fan Kuai!” He then ordered Xiahou Dun to lead troops out on the left and Cao Ren to lead troops out on the right, while Cao Cao himself commanded the center and charged the enemy formation. At a single roll of the drums, all three divisions advanced together. The rebel troops could not withstand them and fled in crushing defeat. Cao Cao personally drew his precious sword and pressed the attack from the rear, leading his men in pursuit and slaughter throughout the night. Vast numbers were killed, and those who surrendered were beyond counting. Li Jue and Guo Si fled westward for their lives, frantic as homeless curs; knowing that they had nowhere left to shelter, they had no choice but to take to the mountains and become bandits.

p.src: One day, the Emperor sent a messenger to Cao Cao’s camp, summoning him to the palace to discuss affairs of state. Hearing that an imperial envoy had arrived, Cao Cao invited him in and received him. He saw that the man had refined features, bright eyes, and a vigorous bearing. Cao Cao thought to himself, “The eastern commanderies are now gripped by famine, and officials, soldiers, and commoners alike look starved. How is this man alone so well fed?” He therefore asked, “Sir, your honored countenance is so full and well nourished. By what regimen have you maintained it?” The man replied, “I have no special method. I have merely eaten plain fare for thirty years.” Cao Cao nodded. Then he asked, “What office do you hold?” He replied, “I was recommended as Filial and Incorrupt. Formerly I served as an aide under Yuan Shao and Zhang Yang. Now, hearing that the Son of Heaven had returned to the capital, I came especially to pay court and was appointed Court Gentleman for Correct Deliberation. I am from Dingtao in Jiyin. My surname is Dong, my given name Zhao, and my courtesy name Gongren.” Cao Cao rose from his mat and said, “I have long heard your distinguished name! How fortunate that I should meet you here.” He then laid out wine in his tent to entertain Dong Zhao and arranged for him to meet Xun Yu. Suddenly, someone reported, “A body of troops is heading east. We do not know whose men they are.” Cao Cao hurriedly sent men to investigate. Dong Zhao said, “Those are Yang Feng, formerly a general under Li Jue, and Han Xian, commander of the White Wave band. Because you have come here, my lord, they are leading their troops away to seek refuge at Daliang.” Cao Cao said, “Can it be that they distrust me?” Dong Zhao replied, “They are men without strategy. Why should you trouble yourself over them, my lord?” Cao Cao asked again, “What will become of the two villains Li Jue and Guo Si now that they have fled?” Dong Zhao said, “A tiger without claws, birds without wings—they will soon be captured by you, my lord. They are not worth another thought.”

p.src: Finding Dong Zhao’s words much to his liking, Cao Cao asked his counsel on the great affairs of the court. Dong Zhao said, “You raised a righteous army to put down tyranny and disorder, my lord, and entered the court to support the Son of Heaven. This is an achievement worthy of the Five Hegemons. Yet the generals all have different purposes and may not submit to you. If you remain here now, I fear it may prove disadvantageous. The best policy is to move the imperial carriage to the capital at Xu. However, the court has wandered in exile and only lately returned to the capital. People near and far look to it, hoping for a day of peace. If the imperial carriage is moved again now, it will not satisfy the hearts of the people. Yet extraordinary deeds alone bring extraordinary achievements. I pray you resolve upon it, General.” Cao Cao took Dong Zhao’s hand and said with a smile, “That has been my own intention from the beginning. But Yang Feng has deployed his forces at Daliang, and the great ministers remain at court. Might some new disturbance arise?” Dong Zhao replied, “That is easily managed. Send Yang Feng a letter first to put his mind at ease. Then state plainly to the ministers that the capital lacks provisions and that you wish the imperial carriage to proceed to Xu, which lies near Luyang and can readily receive transported grain, thus avoiding anxiety over shortages and distance. When the ministers hear this, they will gladly consent.” Cao Cao was delighted. Dong Zhao thanked him and took his leave. Cao Cao held his hand and said, “Whenever I have some design in mind, I shall rely upon your instruction.” Dong Zhao expressed his thanks and departed.

p.src: From then on, Cao Cao conferred secretly each day with his advisers about moving the capital. At that time, Wang Li, Palace Attendant and Grand Astrologer, privately told Liu Ai, Minister of the Imperial Clan, “I have observed the heavens. Since last spring, Venus has trespassed against Saturn in the constellations Dipper and Ox, then crossed the Celestial Ford; Mars has also moved retrograde and met Venus at the Celestial Gate. When metal and fire conjoin, a new Son of Heaven must arise. I perceive that the allotted span of the Great Han is nearing its end; in the lands of Jin and Wei, one is certain to rise.” He also submitted a secret memorial to Emperor Xian: “Heaven’s Mandate passes from one house to another, and none of the Five Phases flourishes forever. That which succeeds fire is earth. The one who replaces Han and possesses all under Heaven should arise in Wei.” When Cao Cao heard this, he sent word to Wang Li: “I know, sir, that you are loyal to the court, but the Way of Heaven is profound and remote. Pray say no more.” Cao Cao related the matter to Xun Yu. Xun Yu said, “Han rules by the virtue of fire, while you, my lord, are destined under earth. Xu belongs to earth; once you reach it, you are certain to prosper. Fire can engender earth, and earth can make wood flourish. This accords precisely with the words of Dong Zhao and Wang Li. In days to come, one is surely destined to rise.” Cao Cao’s mind was thus made up. The next day, he entered the Emperor’s presence and memorialized: “The eastern capital has lain desolate too long and cannot be restored. Moreover, transporting provisions here is exceedingly difficult. Xu lies near Luyang, and its city, palaces, residences, money, grain, people, and goods are amply sufficient for our needs. I venture to request that Your Majesty proceed to Xu. I pray that you consent.” The Emperor dared not refuse. All the ministers feared Cao Cao’s power, and none dared voice a contrary opinion. An auspicious day was therefore chosen for the imperial departure. Cao Cao led his army as escort, and all the officials followed. Before they had traveled many stages, they came to a high ridge. Suddenly, tremendous shouts arose as Yang Feng and Han Xian led troops out to block the road. Xu Huang rode at their head and shouted, “Where are you taking the Emperor, Cao Cao, after abducting him?”

Cao Cao gladly sent him forth.

p.src: That night, Man Chong disguised himself as a common soldier and mingled with the enemy ranks. Stealing up to Xu Huang’s tent, he saw him seated in armor, holding a candle. Man Chong suddenly stepped before him, bowed, and said, “My old friend, have you been well since we parted?” Xu Huang rose in surprise, peered closely at him, and said, “Are you not Man Boning of Shanyang? How have you come here?” Man Chong replied, “I now serve as an aide under General Cao. Today I saw my old friend before the battle lines. I wished to offer you a word of counsel, and so I came especially, risking death.” Xu Huang invited him to sit and asked the purpose of his visit. Man Chong said, “Your courage and strategy are rarely matched in this world. Why do you humble yourself beneath the likes of Yang Feng and Han Xian? General Cao is a hero of our age, and his love of worthy men and courtesy toward scholars are known throughout the realm. When he saw your valor before the lines today, he felt the greatest esteem and admiration. Unwilling to force so valiant a general into a fight to the death, he sent me especially to invite you. Why do you not forsake darkness and turn toward the light, so that together we may accomplish a great enterprise?”

p.src: Xu Huang pondered for a long while, then sighed deeply and said, “I have always known that Yang Feng and Han Xian are not men capable of founding a great cause. Yet I have followed them so long that I cannot bear to abandon them.” Man Chong said, “Have you not heard, ‘A fine bird chooses the tree in which it roosts; a worthy minister chooses the lord whom he serves’? To encounter a lord worthy of service and let the chance slip past is not the act of a true man.” Xu Huang rose, thanked him, and said, “I shall follow your counsel.” Man Chong said, “Why not kill Yang Feng and Han Xian before you leave and offer their heads as your gift of introduction?” Xu Huang replied, “For a subject to murder his lord is a monstrous injustice. I will never do it.” Man Chong said, “You are truly a righteous man!” Xu Huang then led several dozen horsemen of his personal retinue and, together with Man Chong, went over to Cao Cao that very night. Someone had already reported the matter to Yang Feng. Yang Feng flew into a rage and personally led a thousand horsemen in pursuit, shouting, “Xu Huang, you traitorous villain! Do not flee!”

p.src: In the midst of the pursuit, a cannon suddenly boomed. Torches flared all over the hills and valleys, and ambushing troops poured out on every side. Cao Cao himself led the troops at their head and thundered, “I have been waiting here a long time! Let none escape!” Yang Feng was greatly alarmed and hastened to turn his force back, but Cao Cao’s troops had already surrounded him. Just then Han Xian arrived with troops to rescue him. The two armies fell into a confused melee, and Yang Feng escaped. Taking advantage of the enemy’s confusion, Cao Cao pressed his attack, and more than half the soldiers of the two commanders surrendered. Isolated and weakened, Yang Feng and Han Xian led their defeated remnants away to join Yuan Shu.

p.src: Cao Cao recalled his army and returned to camp, where Man Chong brought Xu Huang in to meet him. Cao Cao was overjoyed and treated Xu Huang with great generosity. He then escorted the imperial carriage to Xu, where palaces and halls were constructed, the ancestral temple and altars of soil and grain established, government ministries, offices, and courts founded, and the city walls, official residences, and storehouses repaired. Dong Cheng and twelve others, thirteen men in all, were enfeoffed as marquises. The rewarding of merit and punishment of crime were alike placed at Cao Cao’s disposal.

p.src: Cao Cao appointed himself General-in-Chief and Marquis of Wuping, and made Xun Yu Palace Attendant and Prefect of the Masters of Writing; Xun You was made military adviser; Guo Jia was made Major and Libationer; Liu Ye was made an aide in the Ministry of Works; Mao Jie and Ren Jun were made Household Generals of Agricultural Administration, charged with overseeing funds and provisions; Cheng Yu was made Chancellor of Dongping, while Fan Cheng and Dong Zhao were appointed magistrates of Luoyang; Man Chong was made magistrate of the capital at Xu; Xiahou Dun, Xiahou Yuan, Cao Ren, and Cao Hong were all appointed generals; Lü Qian, Li Dian, Yue Jin, Yu Jin, and Xu Huang were all appointed colonels; Xu Chu and Dian Wei were both appointed commandants; The remaining officers and soldiers each received an appointment. From that time onward, all great authority rested in Cao Cao's hands. All important affairs of the court were first reported to Cao Cao and only then presented to the Emperor.

p.src: After Cao Cao had settled these great affairs, he held a banquet in the rear hall, gathered his advisers, and said, "Liu Bei has stationed his forces in Xuzhou and assumed command of the province himself. Recently, Lü Bu sought refuge with him after a military defeat, and Bei established him at Xiaopei. If the two unite and lead their armies against us, they will become a mortal threat. What ingenious plan have you gentlemen for dealing with them?" Xu Chu said, "Grant me fifty thousand picked troops, and I shall cut off the heads of Liu Bei and Lü Bu and present them to the Chancellor." Xun Yu said, "The general is brave indeed, but he does not understand strategy. The capital at Xu has only just been pacified; we must not resort to arms rashly. I have a plan called 'Two Tigers Contending for Food.' Although Liu Bei now governs Xuzhou, he has received no imperial appointment. My lord should petition for an edict formally appointing Bei Governor of Xuzhou, and secretly enclose a letter instructing him to kill Lü Bu. If he succeeds, Bei will lose a fierce warrior's aid and can gradually be dealt with in turn; if he fails, Lü Bu will surely kill Bei; this is the plan of 'Two Tigers Contending for Food.'" Cao Cao accepted his advice and immediately petitioned for an imperial decree. He sent an envoy bearing it to Xuzhou, appointing Liu Bei General Who Subdues the East, Marquis of Yichengting, and Governor of Xuzhou; he also enclosed a secret letter.

p.src: Now Liu Xuande was in Xuzhou. When he heard that the Emperor had moved to the capital at Xu, he was just preparing a memorial of congratulation. Suddenly it was reported that an imperial envoy had arrived. Xuande went beyond the walls to welcome him, escorted him into the city, received the gracious decree with due obeisance, and then gave a banquet for the envoy. The envoy said, "My lord, you owe this gracious appointment entirely to General Cao's recommendation before the Emperor." Xuande expressed his thanks. The envoy then took out the private letter and handed it to Xuande. After reading it, Xuande said, "This matter still requires deliberation." When the banquet ended, the envoy was lodged at the posthouse. That night, Xuande discussed the matter with his companions. Zhang Fei said, "Lü Bu is a man without honor. What harm is there in killing him?" Xuande said, "He came to me for refuge when he was in desperate straits. If I killed him, I too would be without honor." Zhang Fei said, "It is hard to be a good man!" Xuande would not heed him.

p.src: The next day, Lü Bu came to offer congratulations, and Xuande ordered that he be admitted. Lü Bu said, "I heard that you received a gracious appointment from the court, and have come especially to congratulate you." Xuande modestly thanked him. Suddenly Zhang Fei appeared, sword in hand, and rushed into the hall to kill Lü Bu, but Xuande hastily restrained him. Greatly alarmed, Lü Bu said, "Yide, why are you so determined to kill me?" Zhang Fei cried, "Cao Cao says you are a man without honor and told my elder brother to kill you!" Xuande repeatedly shouted at him to withdraw. Then he led Lü Bu into the rear hall and truthfully explained all that had happened; he also showed Lü Bu the secret letter Cao Cao had sent. After reading it, Lü Bu wept and said, "That villain Cao merely wishes to set the two of us at odds!" Xuande said, "Brother, do not worry. I, Liu Bei, swear never to commit such a dishonorable deed."

p.src: Lü Bu bowed repeatedly in gratitude. Bei kept Lü Bu there to drink, and only in the evening did he return. Guan Yu and Zhang Fei said, "Elder brother, why did you not kill Lü Bu?" Xuande said, "Cao Mengde fears that Lü Bu and I will join forces against him. Therefore he devised this scheme to make the two of us devour each other while he reaps the profit between us. How could we allow ourselves to be used by him?" Lord Guan nodded and agreed. Zhang Fei said, "I only want to kill this villain and put an end to future trouble!" Xuande said, "That is not the deed of a true man."

p.src: The next day, Xuande sent the imperial envoy back to the capital. He submitted a memorial of thanks and also sent Cao Cao a reply saying only that the matter should be deferred until it could be undertaken. The envoy returned to Cao Cao and reported that Xuande had not killed Lü Bu. Cao Cao asked Xun Yu, "This plan has failed. What are we to do?" Xun Yu said, "I have another plan, called 'Driving the Tiger to Devour the Wolf.'" Cao Cao said, "How does the plan work?" Xun Yu said, "Secretly send someone to make contact with Yuan Shu and report that Liu Bei has submitted a confidential memorial seeking to seize the commanderies of the south. When Yuan Shu hears this, he will surely become enraged and attack Bei. My lord can then issue an open imperial decree commanding Liu Bei to campaign against Yuan Shu. When the two sides clash, Lü Bu will surely conceive other ambitions. This is the plan of 'Driving the Tiger to Devour the Wolf.'" Cao Cao was delighted and first dispatched a man to Yuan Shu; then he forged an imperial edict and sent another man to Xuzhou.

p.src: He therefore mustered his troops and horses and fixed a day for departure. Sun Qian said, "We should first decide who is to defend the city." Xuande said, "Which of my two brothers can defend it?" Lord Guan said, "I am willing to defend this city." Xuande said, "I need to consult you morning and evening. How could we be parted?" First, after drinking you become violent and flog the soldiers; second, you act rashly and refuse to heed advice. I cannot set my mind at ease."

He is to see that you drink little at all times, lest some mishap occur." Chen Deng agreed. p.src: Now when Yuan Shu heard that Liu Bei had submitted a memorial seeking to swallow up his prefectures and counties, he flew into a rage and said, "You are nothing but a mat-weaver and sandal-maker, yet now you have brazenly occupied a great commandery and placed yourself among the feudal lords. I was just about to attack you, yet you would plot against me first! How utterly hateful!" He then ordered his senior general Ji Ling to raise one hundred thousand troops and charge toward Xuzhou. The two armies met at Xuyi. Xuande, having fewer troops, encamped with a mountain behind him and a river beside him.

p.src: Ji Ling was a native of Shandong and wielded a three-pointed blade weighing fifty catties. That day he led out his troops and shouted abuse: “Liu Bei, you village lout! How dare you invade my territory!” Xuande said, “I bear the Son of Heaven’s edict to punish disloyal subjects. Now you dare oppose me; even death cannot expiate your crime!” Ji Ling flew into a rage, spurred his horse, brandished his blade, and charged straight at Xuande. Lord Guan roared, “You wretch, cease your insolence!” He rode out and fought a great battle with Ji Ling. They fought thirty bouts in succession, with neither gaining the advantage. Ji Ling called loudly for a brief rest. Lord Guan wheeled his horse back toward his lines and waited before the ranks. Ji Ling instead sent his deputy Xun Zheng into the field. Lord Guan said, “Send only Ji Ling. I will settle with him which of us is the better man!” Xun Zheng said, “You are merely an obscure lesser officer, no match for General Ji!” Lord Guan was enraged and charged straight at Xun Zheng; at the first crossing of horses, he cut Xun Zheng down from the saddle. Xuande drove his troops forward in the attack. Ji Ling suffered a crushing defeat and withdrew to hold the mouth of the Huaiyin River, not daring to offer battle; he merely sent soldiers to raid the camp by stealth, but every attempt was beaten back by the troops of Xuzhou. The two armies remained locked in opposition, of which no more need be said here.

Zhang Fei flew into a rage and cried, “At first I had no wish to beat you;
but since you invoke Lü Bu to frighten me, I am all the more determined to beat you!
When I beat you, I am beating Lü Bu himself!”
No one could dissuade him.
He had Cao Bao flogged fifty strokes and stopped only after everyone pleaded desperately for mercy.

p.src: When the banquet ended, Cao Bao returned home deeply resentful of Zhang Fei. That very night he sent a messenger bearing a letter straight to Xiaopei to see Lü Bu, relating in full Zhang Fei’s outrageous conduct; he also wrote that Xuande had already gone to Huainan, and that Lü Bu should take advantage of Zhang Fei’s drunkenness that very night to lead troops in an assault on Xuzhou, lest the opportunity be lost. On reading the letter, Lü Bu immediately summoned Chen Gong for counsel. Chen Gong said, “Xiaopei was never a place in which to remain for long. Now that Xuzhou presents an opening, if we fail to seize it, regrets will come too late.”

p.src: Lü Bu followed his advice, armed himself, mounted at once, and rode ahead with five hundred cavalry; he ordered Chen Gong to follow with the main army, while Gao Shun also advanced behind them. Xiaopei lay only forty or fifty li from Xuzhou, a journey soon made on horseback. When Lü Bu reached the city walls it was just the fourth watch. The moon shone clear, and the men atop the walls noticed nothing. At the gate Lü Bu called out, “An envoy bearing secret intelligence from Governor Liu has arrived.” Cao Bao’s soldiers on the wall reported this to Cao Bao. He climbed the wall to look, then ordered the soldiers to open the gate. At a signal from Lü Bu, all his soldiers poured in together and raised a tremendous battle cry.

p.src: Zhang Fei lay drunk in his residence. His attendants hurriedly shook him awake and reported, “Lü Bu has tricked them into opening the gate and is fighting his way into the city!” Zhang Fei was furious. He hastily donned his armor and snatched up his eighteen-foot serpent-headed spear; but scarcely had he left the residence and mounted his horse when Lü Bu’s troops arrived and confronted him head-on. Zhang Fei was still not sober and could not fight with all his strength. Lü Bu had long known Zhang Fei’s valor and did not dare press him too hard. Eighteen horsemen from Yan guarded Zhang Fei as he fought his way out through the east gate; Xuande’s family remained in the residence, and he had no time to attend to them.

p.src: Now Cao Bao saw that Zhang Fei had only a dozen or so guards and, counting on his drunkenness, led a hundred-odd men in pursuit. When Zhang Fei saw Cao Bao, he flew into a rage and spurred his horse to meet him. After three bouts Cao Bao turned and fled. Zhang Fei pursued him to the riverbank and thrust his spear squarely into Cao Bao’s back, sending both man and horse to their deaths in the river. Outside the city Zhang Fei rallied the soldiers, and all who escaped the city followed him toward Huainan. Lü Bu entered the city and reassured the inhabitants. He stationed a hundred soldiers to guard the gate of Xuande’s residence and forbade anyone to enter without authority.

p.src: Now Zhang Fei led several dozen horsemen straight to Xuyi to see Xuande and told him in detail how Cao Bao had colluded with Lü Bu from within and without to seize Xuzhou by night. Everyone turned pale. Xuande sighed and said, “What cause is gain for joy, or loss for sorrow?” Lord Guan asked, “Where are our sisters-in-law?” Zhang Fei replied, “They are all trapped inside the city.” Xuande fell silent and said nothing. Lord Guan stamped his foot and reproached him: “When you first asked to defend the city, what did you say? What instructions did our elder brother give you? Today the city is lost and our sisters-in-law are trapped. What are we to do now?” Hearing this, Zhang Fei was so ashamed and terrified that he could find no place to hide; he drew his sword to cut his own throat. Indeed:
